text: Which turn-timer values should the setup screen offer?

options.label: Off, 1, 5, 10 min now; 30 min and 1 h shown disabled as online play (coming later)
options.rationale: On a shared PC clocks run one after another, so 30 min or 1 h per player makes turns of hours; those suit remote play.

options.label: All six values (Off, 1, 5, 10, 30 min, 1 h) available now
Off, 5, 10 min only; add the rest with online play
Drop this idea or defer it to online play

text: On a shared PC, when does a player's clock run?

options.label: Only on their own planning screen; it starts when they press Continue on the handoff screen
options.rationale: The handoff screen shows no map, so stopping the clock there costs nothing and is fair to whoever must walk over to the device.

options.label: From the moment their handoff screen appears
Untimed handoff, but the clock starts by itself after 60 seconds on the handoff screen
One shared clock for the whole turn, split across all local players

text: When a player's time runs out, what gets submitted?

options.label: The orders already planned; every other army holds (entrench or rest); a half-built order is dropped
options.rationale: This is exactly what End Turn does today and matches 'autosubmitted'. webDiplomacy keeps saved orders at the deadline (from recall, unverified).

options.label: Nothing: every army holds (Diplomacy no-orders style)
The computer player plans the armies that have no order
One grace extension per game (the clock restarts once), then the planned orders

text: Can a timed game be paused?

options.label: Yes: a Pause button covers the map like the handoff screen and keeps the same remaining time
options.rationale: Real interruptions happen at a shared PC; hiding the map stops pause from being a free planning extension.

options.label: Yes, but a limited number of pauses per player per game
Yes, and the map stays visible while paused
No pause

text: Does unused time carry over to later turns?

options.label: No: every turn gets the full time again
options.rationale: Simplest to explain and test; no bank state to show.

options.label: Yes: unused time rolls over, as in Polytopia Live games
Chess-clock style: a game-long bank plus a fixed increment each turn (Fischer)

text: Should turn 1 get extra time, since it includes reading the Briefing?

options.label: Yes: turn 1 gets double the chosen time
options.rationale: A 1 or 5 minute clock is tight when the player is also reading the objective and the first-turn hint.

options.label: No: every turn has the same time
Turn 1 is always untimed

text: What should players see about running out of time? Choose all that apply.

options.label: Countdown chip on the planning screen, warnings at 1 minute and 10 seconds, and a line in the turn results saying whose time ran out and how many armies held
options.rationale: Public timeouts explain surprising holds without revealing any orders.

options.label: A sound at 10 seconds
A visible lock-status row showing which players are still planning, as plan.md section 4 describes
A count of each player's timeouts so far this game

text: Should Milestone 3 include weather, and in which form?

options.label: Yes: seasonal weather tables for each climate zone, rolled each turn and shown before planning
options.rationale: Guadalajara, Teruel, and the postponed Catalonia offensive show weather mattered, mostly in winter, and Spain's climates differ too much for one roll.

options.label: Yes, but one weather roll per turn for all of Spain
A fixed seasonal rule with no roll (for example, winter attacks -1 in the interior and north)
Drop this idea or defer it until movement points (idea 6) and aircraft (idea 8) exist
Four zones: Cantabrian, Meseta (interior and Aragon), Mediterranean, South (Andalucia, Extremadura, Ceuta, Melilla)
options.rationale: Each matches a distinct climate in the AEMET normals while keeping only four badges on the map.

options.label: Three zones: North, Interior, South
Every territory rolls its own weather
One zone for all of Spain

text: When do players learn the weather?

options.label: The turn's weather is rolled before planning and shown; the next turn's odds are shown as a forecast
options.rationale: Weather becomes a planning input rather than a surprise, and the odds come straight from the public table.

options.label: This turn's weather and next turn's actual weather are both known
Only a forecast is shown; the actual weather is rolled during resolution and may differ
Weather is revealed only in the turn results
Clear, Hot, Rain, Mud, Snow, Severe cold
options.rationale: Covers every effect seen in the Spanish record (Ebro heat, Guadalajara mud and sleet, Teruel snow and cold); with the soft effect set Hot and Rain show on the map but change no rule until ideas 6 and 8.

options.label: Clear, Rain, Mud, Snow (no Hot, no Severe cold)
Good and Bad only, as in some board wargames

text: Which weather effects should Milestone 3 implement? Choose all that apply.

options.label: A named attack-roll modifier for the battle's zone, plus no digging-in gain in Snow and Severe cold; air and movement effects wait for ideas 8 and 6
options.rationale: These attach to rules that exist today (M14, M22); every move is one connection, so movement costs have nothing to change yet.

options.label: Aircraft grounded in Mud and Snow, except from cities with paved airfields (needs aircraft, idea 8)
Movement costs doubled in Mud and Snow (needs movement points, idea 6)
Sea connections (Strait, Baleares) closed in storms
Armies that move in Severe cold lose men to frostbite
Defenders' works also weakened in Mud

text: How strong should weather's attack modifiers be? (Values are on the d20 ladder from idea 9, which lands first; the d6 equivalent is in brackets.)

options.label: Soft: Hot 0, Rain 0, Mud -3, Snow -3, Severe cold -6 (d6: 0, 0, -1, -1, -2)
options.rationale: 58 percent of soak games already contain a five-turn freeze; soft values hurt attacks only in real winter weather. Hot and Rain are display-only until ideas 6 and 8 land, and can be raised after a harness run.

options.label: Standard: Hot -3, Rain -3, Mud -6, Snow -6, Severe cold -6 (d6: -1, -1, -2, -2, -2)
Movement effects only; no attack modifiers

text: How should the turn's date be shown? (Turn length itself is Q-TEN-4.)

options.label: Yes: two-week turns from 31 July 1936, shown as a date range (Turn 5, 25 Sep to 8 Oct 1936); a turn's month is its midpoint's month
options.rationale: Weather odds need a month, and dates let players connect turns to history (Guadalajara is turns 16-17).

options.label: Show only the month and season, not exact dates
Keep the date on turn 1 only (today's rule B15) and track the month internally

text: Should the tables be purely random, or follow the historical weather?

options.label: Purely random from the seasonal tables, seeded per game
options.rationale: Keeps one generic mechanism; a scripted 1937-38 Teruel winter would be scenario-specific code or data with no other use yet.

options.label: Random, but force known historical events (for example the Teruel blizzard of 31 Dec 1937 to 3 Jan 1938)
Fully scripted historical weather for every turn
